source.title: Mr. Charles W. Ergen Chairman of the Board of Directors EchoStar Corporation 9601 South Meridian Boulevard Englewood, Colorado 80112 RE: EchoStar’s Spectrum Licenses Dear Mr. Ergen: The FCC has an obligation to ensure that the companies we regulate comply with the terms of their federal spectrum licenses. As you know, EchoStar or its affiliated companies hold a large number of FCC spectrum licenses that cover a significant amount of spectrum. I am therefore writing to inform you that I have asked the FCC’s staff to take several steps regarding spectrum licenses that your companies hold. Specifically, I have directed agency staff to begin a review of EchoStar’s compliance with its federal obligations to provide 5G service throughout the United States per the terms of its federal spectrum licenses. As you know, buildout obligations are one way that the FCC can ensure that Americans, including those living in rural communities, have a fair shot at next-generation connectivity. After all, failure to meet buildout obligations leaves these communities behind. In 2019, EchoStar’s predecessor, DISH, agreed to meet specific buildout obligations in connection with a number of spectrum licenses across several different bands. In particular, the FCC agreed to relax some of EchoStar’s then-existing buildout obligations in exchange for EchoStar’s commitment to put its licensed spectrum to work deploying a nationwide 5G broadband network. EchoStar promised—among other things—that its network would cover, by June 14, 2025, at least 70% of the population within each of its licensed geographic areas for its AWS-4 and 700 MHz licenses, and at least 75% of the population within each of its licensed geographic areas for its H Block and 600 MHz licenses. The terms of the deal were clear. The FCC structured the buildout obligations to prevent spectrum warehousing and to ensure that Americans would gain broader access to high-speed

thesis.thesis: EchoStar’s recent $40 B spectrum sale and strong liquidity position provide a solid foundation for its hybrid MNO transition, but the company faces significant regulatory risk, terminal decline in its core Pay‑TV and broadband businesses, and modest wireless growth that together neutralize the upside, leaving the stock in a balanced position.

drivers.evidence: The sale of 50 MHz to AT&T for ~$23 B and AWS‑4/H‑block to SpaceX for ~$17 B (findings 1,2) was approved by the FCC (finding 3) and resulted in $40 B in proceeds (findings 17,48,64,65).

bull_case.point: EchoStar’s $40 B spectrum sale to AT&T and SpaceX generated a massive cash inflow that eliminated net debt and removed bankruptcy risk, transforming the company’s balance sheet and liquidity position.
bull_case.evidence: The sale of 50 MHz to AT&T for ~$23 B and AWS‑4/H‑block to SpaceX for ~$17 B (findings 1,2) was approved by the FCC (finding 3) and resulted in $40 B in proceeds (findings 17,48,64,65).

bull_case.point: The spectrum sale cleared the way for Boost Mobile to operate as a hybrid MNO, integrating with AT&T’s network and expanding nationwide coverage while reducing operational costs.
bull_case.evidence: The sale enabled Boost Mobile to become a hybrid carrier using AT&T towers and its own 5G core (finding 4) and the AT&T acquisition expands coverage virtually everywhere (findings 61,62).

bull_case.point: The FCC probe into EchoStar’s 5G obligations was closed, and a 3‑year extension was granted, reducing regulatory risk and allowing the company to focus on deployment.
bull_case.evidence: The FCC ended its probe after the AT&T and SpaceX deals (finding 5) and granted a 3‑year extension to deploy its 5G network (finding 25).

bull_case.point: Market sentiment turned strongly positive: the stock surged 70% after the AT&T deal, and analysts raised price targets to $67 (Deutsche Bank) and $110 (Morgan Stanley).
bull_case.evidence: The stock jump of 70% followed the $23 B sale (finding 6); Deutsche Bank lifted its target to $67 (finding 47); Morgan Stanley upgraded to $110 citing spectrum value and SpaceX exposure (finding 54).

bull_case.point: EchoStar now owns a significant equity stake in SpaceX—$8.5 B in stock, up 308% YTD—providing upside from SpaceX’s growth trajectory.
bull_case.evidence: The company holds $8.5 B in SpaceX stock (finding 49) and received $11.12 B in SpaceX Class A common stock as part of the deal (finding 34).

bull_case.point: EchoStar Capital was created to invest the proceeds from spectrum transactions into growth initiatives, positioning the company for future expansion.
bull_case.evidence: The new division EchoStar Capital was established to invest capital from spectrum transactions (finding 35).

bear_case.point: EchoStar’s FY2025 net loss of $14.5 B and lack of sufficient cash to fund obligations over the next 12 months raise substantial doubt about its going‑concern status.
bear_case.evidence: FY2025 net loss was $14.5B; EchoStar warned substantial doubt about its going‑concern status, lacking cash and projected cash flows to fund obligations over the next 12 months.

thesis.confidence_why: The evidence is evenly split between decisive tailwinds and headwinds, with macro conditions neutral, resulting in a balanced view that is moderately confident.

snapshot_notes: S&P above bear level (pro bull definition)
macro.narrative: The expansionary ISM data and upward‑sloping yield curve signal a robust macro backdrop that should lift end‑market demand for EchoStar’s wireless and enterprise services, while the low VIX and strong equity bias reduce financing costs. However, the company’s core pay‑TV and broadband businesses remain in terminal decline, so pricing power is unlikely to improve. The improved credit environment may ease working‑capital constraints and support the company’s ability to service debt, but the high debt load and recent FCC review still pose risks.

implications.why: Expanding PMI and new orders suggest higher consumer and business spending on communications, boosting demand for EchoStar’s wireless and enterprise services.
An upward‑sloping yield curve and low VIX imply lower borrowing rates, reducing EchoStar’s interest expense and easing debt servicing.
Improved credit conditions and higher demand should increase cash inflows, strengthening EchoStar’s working‑capital position.
Enterprise order backlog grew 8% to $1.6B, indicating stronger future revenue streams amid macro expansion.
EchoStar’s spectrum sale reduces future capex needs, but the company may still need to invest in 5G build‑out, which could strain cash.
Terminal decline in pay‑TV and broadband limits EchoStar’s ability to raise prices, so pricing power remains weak.

source.title: Mr. Charles W. Ergen Chairman of the Board of Directors EchoStar Corporation 9601 South Meridian Boulevard Englewood, Colorado 80112 RE: EchoStar’s Spectrum Licenses Dear Mr. Ergen: The FCC has an obligation to ensure that the companies we regulate comply with the terms of their federal spectrum licenses. As you know, EchoStar or its affiliated companies hold a large number of FCC spectrum licenses that cover a significant amount of spectrum. I am therefore writing to inform you that I have asked the FCC’s staff to take several steps regarding spectrum licenses that your companies hold. Specifically, I have directed agency staff to begin a review of EchoStar’s compliance with its federal obligations to provide 5G service throughout the United States per the terms of its federal spectrum licenses. As you know, buildout obligations are one way that the FCC can ensure that Americans, including those living in rural communities, have a fair shot at next-generation connectivity. After all, failure to meet buildout obligations leaves these communities behind. In 2019, EchoStar’s predecessor, DISH, agreed to meet specific buildout obligations in connection with a number of spectrum licenses across several different bands. In particular, the FCC agreed to relax some of EchoStar’s then-existing buildout obligations in exchange for EchoStar’s commitment to put its licensed spectrum to work deploying a nationwide 5G broadband network. EchoStar promised—among other things—that its network would cover, by June 14, 2025, at least 70% of the population within each of its licensed geographic areas for its AWS-4 and 700 MHz licenses, and at least 75% of the population within each of its licensed geographic areas for its H Block and 600 MHz licenses. The terms of the deal were clear. The FCC structured the buildout obligations to prevent spectrum warehousing and to ensure that Americans would gain broader access to high-speed
